questions.q: A function is promised to be either constant or balanced, and you must decide which using oracle queries. Which algorithm applies, and what is the exact query gap?
options: Deutsch-Jozsa; 1 quantum query vs. 2^(n-1)+1 classical worst-case queries
Quantum walk search; a quadratic hitting-time speedup
HHL; a polylogarithmic speedup conditional on state preparation
Simon's algorithm; O(n) quantum queries vs. Omega(2^(n/2)) classical queries
questions.explain: The constant-vs-balanced promise is exactly Deutsch-Jozsa's problem, solved with exactly 1 quantum query vs. 2^(n-1)+1 classical queries in the worst case.

questions.q: A 2-to-1 function hides an XOR mask s that must be recovered via oracle queries. Which algorithm applies, and is its speedup quadratic or exponential?
options: Deutsch-Jozsa; the speedup is a fixed gap of 1 vs. 2 queries only
HHL; the speedup is polylogarithmic in the matrix dimension
Simon's algorithm; the speedup is exponential -- O(n) quantum queries vs. a proven Omega(2^(n/2)) classical lower bound
Quantum walk search; the speedup is quadratic, identical to Grover's
questions.explain: This is Simon's problem, and its gap is exponential -- a proven classical lower bound of Omega(2^(n/2)) against O(n) quantum queries, qualitatively stronger than a quadratic speedup.

questions.q: Someone claims 'HHL exponentially speeds up solving any system of linear equations.' Which caveats from this chapter make 'any' and 'exponentially' both wrong as stated?
options: HHL provides no speedup whatsoever under any circumstances, so both words are simply false
HHL only works for matrices that are not Hermitian, so 'any system' is actually understated
There are no real caveats; the claim as stated is fully accurate

The advantage depends on efficient state preparation of b, a favorable (small) condition number kappa, and a readout need limited to an aggregate quantity rather than the full solution vector -- all three must hold for the exponential comparison to be valid
questions.explain: HHL's log(N) advantage is conditional on cheap state preparation, small condition number, and a narrow readout need -- without all three, the exponential comparison to classical methods doesn't hold.

questions.q: A search algorithm uses a repeated 'coin flip plus shift' step on a graph to find a marked node, instead of amplitude amplification on a flat list. What concept is this, and what is its speedup relative to classical search on the same graph?
options: A quantum walk search; the speedup is quadratic, in the same family as Grover's algorithm (which is itself a special case of quantum walk search)
Deutsch-Jozsa; the speedup is a single fixed query regardless of graph size
HHL; the speedup is polylogarithmic in the graph size
Simon's algorithm; the speedup is exponential
questions.explain: Quantum walk search generalizes Grover's algorithm (itself a special-case quantum walk) and shares its quadratic hitting-time speedup, not an exponential one.

questions.q: Shor's algorithm's period-finding reduction is described as directly inspired by which earlier algorithm, and how do their hidden structures differ?
options: HHL; both produce a quantum state proportional to a classical solution vector
Deutsch-Jozsa; both solve the exact same constant-vs-balanced promise problem
Grover's algorithm; both use amplitude amplification as their core mechanism

Simon's algorithm; both are hidden subgroup problem instances using Fourier-style interference plus classical post-processing, but Simon's recovers a hidden XOR mask over (Z/2)^n while Shor's recovers a hidden period over integers mod N
questions.explain: Simon's algorithm is the direct conceptual ancestor of Shor's period-finding -- both are hidden subgroup problem instances, differing in the algebraic structure (XOR mask vs. period) and the group it's hidden over.
